Succession requires a decision before the king dies

Verse 6 says David never questioned Adonijah about his conduct. Verse 18 says the king does not know what is happening. Bathsheba’s words in verse 20 put the decision where it belongs. All Israel is waiting for David to name his heir. She also names the danger to herself and her son (verse 21). Nathan arranges for two voices to bring the same report (verses 13–14). The oath she cites is not recorded earlier in these books.
The new throne is secured through removals

Each removal in this chapter comes with a stated reason. Adonijah asked for a woman of the late king’s household (verse 22). Joab had killed two commanders in peacetime (verse 32). Shimei broke his sworn terms (verse 43). In verse 26 Abiathar is spared for his years of loyalty to David. Verse 27 links his removal to the word against Eli’s house. The reader sees justice and advantage served by the same acts.
Wisdom begins as a request to hear people well

Solomon calls himself “a little child” in verse 7. His request in verse 9 is for a heart that hears. He wants it in order to judge God’s people, not for himself. Verse 11 lists what he did not ask for: long life, riches, his enemies’ deaths. The first case tests the gift. Two women of low standing come with no witnesses (verse 18). The king hears them and finds the one who loves the child.
Royal abundance requires a system of supply

Verses 22–23 give the court’s food for a single day. Verse 27 says where it came from. Twelve officers collected it, each for one month (verse 7). The chapter also shows general plenty and safety (verses 20 and 25). Both pictures stand together. Samuel warned that a king would “take” fields and produce (1 Samuel 8:14–15). In 12:4 the people call Solomon’s rule a heavy yoke.
The building's beauty depends on counted labor

The temple begins with a trade deal and a labor draft. Verse 13 says the draft came “out of all Israel.” Each man spends one month in Lebanon and two at home (verse 14). Verses 15–16 count the carriers, stonecutters, and overseers. Adoniram, who runs the draft, is stoned in 12:18. Chapter 9:22 says Solomon made no Israelite a bondservant. The book keeps both statements.
A building cannot replace the duties attached to it

The chapter is almost all measurements and materials. Verses 11–13 interrupt it with a message. Verse 12 begins with “if” and names statutes, ordinances, and commandments. The promise to David depends on the king’s conduct. Verse 13 says the LORD will dwell “among the children of Israel.” It does not say he will live in the building. Chapter 9:6–7 states what happens to the house if the condition fails.
A temple depends on skilled workers

Verse 14 introduces the craftsman by his parents. His mother was an Israelite widow, and his father a man of Tyre. The verse says he was filled with wisdom, understanding, and skill. Exodus 31:3 uses the same three terms for Bezalel, who built the tabernacle. So the text counts a metalworker’s skill as a kind of wisdom. A man of two peoples makes the temple’s bronze. The bronze stand shown is a regional comparison, not a temple vessel.
The dedication imagines listeners beyond Israel

Solomon’s prayer lists seven kinds of need. The fifth, in verses 41–43, concerns a person outside Israel. That foreigner has heard of God’s name and comes from far away. Solomon asks God to do all the foreigner requests. The stated aim is that all peoples may know God’s name (verse 43). Verse 27 has already said no house can contain God. Verses 46–50 even expect a day when Israel prays from exile.
The warning imagines the temple as a future ruin

This answer comes just after the temple’s dedication. Verse 3 says God has made the house holy. Verse 7 says that same house can be cast out of his sight. Its holiness comes from God and depends on Israel’s loyalty. Verses 8–9 picture people passing the ruin and asking why. The answer given is that Israel left the LORD for other gods. Second Kings 25:9 reports the day the house was burned.
A visitor's praise presents one view of courtly success

The queen judges the court by what a visitor can see. In verse 8 she calls the servants happy because they hear his wisdom. In verse 9 she states what a king is for: justice and righteousness. The rest of the chapter counts gold, shields, and horses (verses 14–29). Deuteronomy 17:16–17 told kings not to pile up horses, wives, or gold. It names Egypt as the source of horses. The chapter makes no comment, and chapter 11 does.
A divided garment makes a political warning visible

Ahijah acts out his message before he speaks it. The cloak is new, and he tears it into twelve pieces (verse 30). Ten go to Jeroboam, and one tribe stays with David’s house (verses 31–32). The text does not explain the missing piece. A torn robe also marked Saul’s loss of the kingdom (1 Samuel 15:27–28). The reason given is worship of other gods (verse 33). Jeroboam receives a promise with a condition, as David’s house did (verse 38).
The divided kingdom begins with a labor complaint

The people’s request in verse 4 is an offer, not a revolt. They will serve the new king if he eases the labor. The elders see that the king must first serve them (verse 7). Rehoboam chooses the harsh answer in verse 14. Verse 15 adds that the turn of events came from the LORD. The text names both the king’s folly and God’s purpose. The cry in verse 16 repeats Sheba’s words from 2 Samuel 20:1.
An authoritative claim can still deceive

The man of God turned down a king’s reward without trouble (verses 8–9). He gives way to a fellow prophet. His own command came to him directly (verse 9). The new one comes secondhand, and it reverses the first. Verse 18 says plainly, “He lied to him,” and gives no motive. Strangely, the liar then speaks a true word (verses 20–22). The lion kills but does not eat, which marks a sign (verse 28).
Disguise cannot control the answer sought

Jeroboam sends to the prophet who once promised him a kingdom (verse 2). He hides who is asking. The disguise is useless twice: Ahijah is blind and has been told (verses 4–5). Verse 6 greets her by name at the door. She came for a word about one child and hears about a whole house. The boy dies as her feet cross the threshold (verse 17). Verse 13 calls his burial a kindness, since something good was found in him.
An alliance purchases relief by changing another ruler's loyalties

Asa is one of the kings this book praises (verses 11–14). His answer to a border threat is to buy a foreign army. The payment in verse 18 comes from the temple’s own treasure. Verse 19 asks Ben Hadad to break his treaty with Israel. The plan works (verses 20–22). The price is paid by Israelite towns in the north. Second Chronicles 16:7–9 records a prophet’s rebuke for this bargain.
A new capital survives rapid changes of rulers

This chapter moves through five rulers in thirty-four verses. Three of them die by violence or fire. Verse 24 records the one act of Omri that lasts. He buys a hill at a fair price and names the city for its seller. Samaria remains the capital until the kingdom falls (2 Kings 17:5–6). The book judges Omri only by his worship (verses 25–26). Verse 34 ties Jericho’s rebuilding to Joshua’s curse (Joshua 6:26).
A prophet depends on a household already facing hunger

Zarephath belongs to Sidon (verse 9), the homeland of Jezebel (16:31). The prophet is sent outside Israel to be fed. His host is a widow with one handful of meal (verse 12). She speaks of “the LORD your God,” not her own. Elijah asks her to feed him first and gives a promise (verses 13–14). Verse 15 says she went and did it. Jesus later cites her in Luke 4:25–26.
A public question frames the contest as a choice

Elijah’s question in verse 21 allows no middle position. The people say nothing, since they have been keeping both. He then sets terms that favor the other side. Baal’s prophets are many, go first, and have most of the day (verses 22–29). Elijah soaks his own offering three times (verses 33–35). His prayer is short and asks that the people may know (verses 36–37). In verse 39 the silent crowd finally answers.
Elijah's isolation differs from the larger situation described

Elijah says twice that he alone is left (verses 10 and 14). The quiet voice between them does not change his words. The LORD’s first answer to his despair was food and sleep (verses 5–7). The second is work: three people to anoint (verses 15–16). Verse 18 then corrects his count with seven thousand. Obadiah’s hundred prophets were also still alive (18:13). In Elisha he is given a successor.
A victorious treaty receives a different prophetic judgment

A prophet said the victory was given so Israel would know the LORD (verse 28). Ahab treats it as a chance for trade. Verse 34 lists his gains: towns returned and markets in Damascus. He frees the king on those terms. The prophet’s staged case works as Nathan’s story did (verses 39–40). Ahab passes sentence on himself. Verse 42 says the man he released was not his to release.
An inherited field is more than a commodity

Ahab’s offer in verse 2 is fair as a sale. Naboth’s refusal in verse 3 rests on something else. The field is his fathers’ inheritance, and he calls on the LORD. Leviticus 25:23 and Numbers 36:7 keep such land within the family. Ahab sulks (verse 4), and Jezebel asks whether he rules Israel (verse 7). The tablet shows an ordinary field sale, the kind Naboth refuses. She then uses Israel’s own court forms, with two witnesses, to kill (verses 9–10).
The court pressures a speaker to match an approved answer

The messenger in verse 13 means well. He asks Micaiah to agree with the four hundred. Micaiah answers that he will say what the LORD says (verse 14). Ahab himself knows the first cheerful answer is false (verse 16). He demands the truth and has already said he hates it (verse 8). He jails the man who gives it (verse 27). The disguise fails against an arrow shot “at random” (verse 34).
